header:
Date: 2025-10-21
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 43 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jules Nguyen (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Elysian Head of Platform), Devon Clarke (Elysian ML Eng), Priya Nair (Elysian Security)
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to keep todays focused, token econ results and a couple of tuning levers. quick roll call?
[00:12] Marta: Marta here. Devon and Priya too. Marcus might drop in later.
[00:18] Samir: great, cool. Jules you want to kick off with the numbers?
[00:25] Jules: yeah, sure. so uh quick caveat, some of these runs were on a mixed batch of toy traffic and synthetic, so take the absolute numbers with a grain of salt but the relative deltas should hold.
[00:40] Jules: we ran two model variants - rdx-13b-8k-qat and rdx-13b-16k-ql4, and measured tokens per second per dollar using the pilot pricing profile we gave last week. baseline (no caching, batch size 1) rdx-13b-8k came in at ~320 tokens/sec/$, the 16k ql4 was lower — about 260 tokens/sec/$.
[01:05] Devon: out of curiosity are those numbers including NVMe caching overhead? we saw some spikes when the KV spilled to disk.
[01:12] Jules: good catch — these initial runs had minimal disk spill; most of the KV fit in GPU mem for the synthetic traces. we did one stress run where the cache dropped to disk and latency spiked; I have traces in the shared sheet.
[01:25] Samir: link to the sheet is in the notes (redwood.com/shared/elysian-poc-costs) — just a pointer, not public.
[01:32] Marta: ok, so tokens/sec/$ is the main metric we care about. Devon and I talked and our product cares about tail latency more than peak throughput. how do batching changes affect tails?
[01:44] Jules: batching is the main tradeoff — larger batches improve tokens/sec/$ but increase p95/p99. For rdx-13b-8k we saw batch size 4 improved tokens/sec/$ by ~1.9x vs batch 1, but p99 jumped from 220ms to 480ms under the same arrival pattern.
[02:02] Devon: and that's with continuous batching in the runtime, right? not queued batching?
[02:07] Jules: right — continuous batching with a 20ms wait window. if you shrink the wait window you get lower latency but less batching benefit.
[02:14] Priya: quick security Q — when you mention KV cache, is any user PII persisted off-host? Elysian can't have PHI landing on shared disk.
[02:24] Samir: yep, good point. for the hosted pilot we can enable in-memory only KV cache or configure per-customer encryption and HSM-backed KMS. we documented options in the security pack we shared.
[02:36] Priya: can you point me to the exact KMS flow? we need key rotation details and audit logs.
[02:42] Jules: I'll attach the KMS diagram and the audit-log retention table. short answer: we support customer-managed keys, HSM-backed rotation, and the console emits token-level audit events.
[02:52] Marta: back to econ — you mentioned prefix caching gave most of the savings for our dialog traffic?
[02:58] Jules: yes. prefix caching (cache only the first N tokens of a conversation) delivered ~40% cost reduction on our sample chat flows because many prompts re-used the same long system prompt and instruction prefixes. KV cache adds another ~15% in the best case when there is repeated generation over the same context windows.
[03:15] Devon: what's the memory tradeoff for prefix vs full KV?
[03:19] Jules: prefix-only is tiny — couple MBs per conversation. full KV scales with sequence length and number of unique tokens cached; we saw it grow to several GB per GPU when synthetic trace included long multi-turns.
[03:30] Samir: so recommended pattern for now: use prefix caching in hosted pilot to get immediate wins, run a constrained KV config in dedicated if you need big hit-rate for few customers.
[03:43] Marta: ok that fits our org — want predictable economics first. Devon, can you summarize the throughput profile you want?
[03:50] Devon: sure — our baseline QPS target for the pilot is 25 QPS with median response length ~120 tokens, p95 latency <350ms. we can accept higher p99 for background async features but customer-facing chat must be under 500ms p99.
[04:05] Jules: given that, batch size 2 with a 15ms wait window is probably the sweet spot. gives ~1.4x cost improvement vs batch 1 and keeps p95 near your 350ms goal in our runs.
[04:18] Samir: we also tested quantization variants; ql4 saved about 20% cost vs 8-bit QAT in these workloads but had slightly lower output fidelity in the hallucination evals.
[04:30] Devon: did you run any reranking or long-context retrieval flows? our product uses a 2-stage pipeline: short generator and then a reranker. caching interacts with that.
[04:39] Jules: yes, two-stage tests show that caching the generator prefix and reranker inputs reduces total tokens generated by ~22% in our sample, which compounds the savings. we put the reranker on a smaller model to reduce unit cost.
[04:52] Marcus (off): sorry late — quick note, are we looking at dedicated for the pilot or hosted?
[04:56] Samir: right now hosted makes sense to iterate fast; we recommended dedicated if you need guaranteed p95 SLAs or large KV footprint.
[05:04] Marta: what is the break-even for dedicated vs hosted? we have some internal numbers but would like your guidance.
[05:11] Jules: ballpark — for sustained 25 QPS with 120 token med, if you have consistent utilization >60% over a month, dedicated becomes cost-advantageous. but it depends on whether your KV memory needs would push you to multi-GPU rigs. we can model this in the spreadsheet.
[05:28] Devon: can you show the model quickly?
[05:30] Samir: sure — I'm sharing screen (note: transcription autoplace-holder) — in the sheet we compare hosted per-token price vs dedicated amortized node + infra. youll see a dashed line where dedicated crosses hosted cost.
[05:43] Jules: another note: we can compress saved KV using a lossy sketch for tokens with low entropy; that saved ~10% memory in our experiments without affecting generation.
[05:53] Priya: for dedicated, our security team will require network isolation and audit forwarding. does Redwood support per-tenant audit forward?
[06:02] Samir: yes, we can forward audit logs to a customer-owned syslog or cloud logging endpoint; we also support per-tenant RBAC and SSO via SAML.
[06:12] Marta: cool. two quick nitpicks on the numbers: first, those tokens/sec/$ look high compared to our previous platform, are you normalizing for prompt engineering differences?
[06:21] Jules: partly. our runs included standard prompt templates; when we applied your longer system prompts the numbers dropped slightly. that's in the 'by-route' tab.
[06:30] Devon: about the batching tradeoff—if we move to a small edge cache (per-region microcache) how does that change the batching gains?
[06:38] Jules: it tends to reduce arrival variability and smooth bursts, which helps batching; you may see up to 25% higher effective batching because requests aggregate by region. but adds infra complexity.
[06:49] Samir: we should also call out cold-start costs — spinning up GPU-backed dedicated nodes for a low duty cycle can be expensive; warm pools are better.
[06:58] Marta: agreed. can you include warm pool sizing recommendations in the next spreadsheet update?
[07:03] Samir: yes — we'll add recommended pool sizes and an amortized cost calc.
[07:08] Jules: one more experimental item — we saw that adaptive batching (dynamically changing the wait window based on recent arrival rate) yielded ~8-12% extra tokens/sec/$ without hurting tail in our sim. we can test that in your pilot.
[07:21] Devon: sounds promising. do you have an A/B harness? we want clean comparisons.
[07:24] Jules: we can set up parallel routes in the pilot to compare batch configs, and emit route-level cost/latency metrics in the console.
[07:31] Priya: another security Q — retention of audit logs, you said token-level events are emitted. how long are they kept? our legal needs 12 months.
[07:39] Samir: default is 90 days, but enterprise plans can add longer retention as an add-on and we can stream to your long-term store.
[07:46] Marta: ok, last thing — we want a short executive-friendly slide that explains the cost drivers and the recommended next config. can you produce that for next week?
[07:56] Samir: yes, we'll produce a 1-page exec summary and a separate technical playbook.
[08:03] Jules: actionables recap: I'll run the KV cache configs, Samir updates spreadsheet and exec 1-pager, Devon runs batch/throughput tests in staging, Priya sends security checklist items.
[08:13] Devon: timeline check — we should have experiments done and a decision by end of month.
[08:18] Samir: agreed. any blockers?
[08:21] Priya: just the KMS docs and confirmation about no-PHI on shared NVMe — if you can confirm in writing, we'll be comfortable.
[08:30] Jules: will attach the KMS flow and a formal note about in-memory-only KV option.
[08:36] Marta: thanks all, productive. Samir can you email the summary and links after?
[08:41] Samir: yep, sending after. thanks everyone.
[08:44] [TRANSCRIPT NOTES] Occasional automatic speaker mislabels (Marcus sometimes appears as Speaker 3). Some technical terms transcribed imperfectly (ql4 vs ql-4; KV vs K-V). See shared spreadsheet for raw logs and perf traces.
[08:59] [END]
